newsitem.title: USA: Ohio study says LEAP program shows modest results.
newsitem.headline: Ohio study says LEAP program shows modest results.

text.p: A programme that pays teenaged parents to stay in school increases the likelihood they will land jobs and get off welfare, but does not raise high school graduation rates, a study said Wednesday.

Ohio's LEAP programme, an acronym for Learning, Earning and Parenting, was more effective at helping teenaged parents already in school than those who had dropped out and were induced by the programme to return to school, the Manpower Demonstration Research Corporation (MDRC) study said.
"All states will have to do something in this area. The Ohio results suggest these approaches matter, but there are no easy answers," MDRC President Judith Gueron told Reuters.
The Ohio programme provides a $62 stipend to teenaged parents on welfare for each month they attend school regularly, reducing benefits if attendance falls off.
In its fifth and final evaluation, the nonprofit social policy research group examined records on 4,151 teenaged parents, with the control group of teenagers selected from a dozen Ohio counties.

The study found that 23 percent of the young parents in the programme ended up graduating from high school, compared to 23.5 percent in the control group. However, a higher percentage of those already in school when they entered the incentive programme stayed in school, while only about one-third of drop-outs who enrolled in the programme completed their junior year.

The programme produced similar results after high school, with 65 percent of participants who were already in school when enrolled in LEAP reportedly getting jobs during the subsequent four years, compared to 56 percent of drop-outs in the programme.

"Clearly, LEAP's incentives affected teens' behaviour and reduced welfare receipts. But the findings suggest that incentives alone are unlikely to dramatically increase graduation rates -- an important step toward long-term self-sufficiency," Gueron said.

The findings were considered important because a new federal block-grant programme, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, enacted in August distributes federal funds on the basis of whether teenaged parents stay in school until they graduate or meet a high school equivalency standard.
The LEAP programme proved to be cost-effective, the study found, returning 99 cents in savings for every $1 invested.
